questions.q: What actually happens when a BACKUP DATABASE statement lists two DISK = targets, like TO DISK = 'path1', DISK = 'path2'?
options: The backup is striped — split across both files — and all files are required to restore
Two complete, independent copies of the backup are created
The second DISK target is ignored
SQL Server automatically chooses whichever disk has more free space
questions.explain: Multiple DISK targets in one BACKUP statement stripe the backup across them for I/O performance — it is not redundancy, and losing any one file breaks the whole set.

questions.q: How does a mirrored backup (using MIRROR TO) differ from a striped backup?
options: A mirrored backup creates complete, independent copies — losing one still leaves a restorable backup, unlike striping where every file is required
There is no real difference between MIRROR TO and listing multiple DISK targets
Mirrored backups are only available in Standard Edition, unlike striped backups
Mirroring always produces a smaller file than striping
questions.explain: MIRROR TO (Enterprise Edition only) produces genuinely redundant copies; each mirror set must match the primary set's device count.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a backup stored on the same physical disk as the database's data and log files actually protect against?
options: Logical errors like a bad UPDATE or accidental DROP TABLE — but zero protection if that physical disk fails
Every possible failure, including disk failure, since the backup is a separate file
Nothing at all, including logical errors
Only network-based attacks
questions.explain: A same-disk backup can recover from mistakes made in the data, but if the disk itself fails, the backup and the database are lost together.

questions.q: What is a real tradeoff of using a network share as a backup destination instead of local disk?
options: It survives the loss of the database server itself, at the cost of network latency and dependency on the share's own availability
Network shares are always faster to write to than local disk
Network shares eliminate the need for any backup verification
There is no tradeoff — network shares are strictly better in every respect
questions.explain: A network share decouples the backup's survival from the database server's survival, but introduces latency and a new dependency on the share itself.

questions.q: A DBA runs BACKUP DATABASE Sales TO DISK = 'D:\Sales_1.bak', DISK = 'E:\Sales_2.bak' and later loses the E: drive entirely. Can they restore from Sales_1.bak alone?
options: No — this was a striped backup, and all files in the striped set are required to restore; MIRROR TO would have prevented this exposure
Yes — each DISK target in a BACKUP statement is always an independent, complete copy
Yes, but only if the database was in SIMPLE recovery
No — striped backups can never be restored under any circumstances, even with all files intact
questions.explain: Because multiple DISK targets stripe rather than mirror the backup, losing any one file makes the entire striped set unusable — MIRROR TO is the option that creates true redundant copies.
